title: Notes of Ministry - 61 - December 1977

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 61 - December 1 (2430)/Notes of Ministry - 61 - Decemb - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: It may be noticed that the thought of witness arises in these scriptures. The end in mind, which is intimated to us in Acts 1, is that we be Christ’s witnesses; not merely those who speak of Him (though speaking of Him would be of great import), but those who personally are His witnesses. We may well ponder what the hosts of heaven can see as lovers of God continue here, where so much that is not of God is extant. It is not only a matter of what men around us may behold; it is a question of what heaven can see, and what we can see in one another. An occasion like this, which we can fittingly speak of as an occasion for fellowship, involves what we can see and experience in one another.

John especially records, in the verses we read in his first epistle, that God has witness borne to certain things. That is to work out in ourselves severally in the greatest assurance as to the knowledge of God Himself. There are specifically these three things, “For they that bear witness are three—the Spirit, and the water, and the blood”; great matters which faith can always have reference to, that we may be stabilised and strengthened perhaps I could add, energised—to continue in this point of witness. We could never have been fitting witnesses of Christ had He not gone into death. There can never be a fitting witness to Christ in

the order of man that was put away at the cross; that is a point which excludes unregulated so-called evangelical activity. There may be a taking up of Scripture, a reading of Scripture; but the idea of witness runs deep, and relates to the whole person, what a person is, and the company in which that person joins, with many another, in what is just one glorious point of witness—that we are witnesses of Christ.
The water and the blood were in the fullest degree needful, but they stand as witnesses to us.

Christ has died; Jesus has laid down His life; His precious blood has flowed; the blood and the water have flowed from His smitten side to meet the whole state and condition of a man that has fallen into sin, that he might fittingly be a witness to God and to Christ. A witness in the full sense in which I speak of it is not just a question of making right statements. We thank God for every right statement, for every statement which is supported in Scripture and is according to the truth; but the full thought of witness is not just in such statements; it runs deep into the soul of a person, and the company of such persons, witnesses of Christ.

The witnesses from God’s side are three—“the Spirit, and the water, and the blood”. We need the first to understand the second and the third. We need the Spirit rightly to understand the holy significance of the water and the blood. What place has the Spirit with us? The Spirit is witnessing; it is an active thought in relation to the Spirit of God in us. He is bearing witness to things, particularly to a great point which we need to be in the gain of in these closing moments—the matter of eternal life. “This is the witness, that God has given to us eternal life; and this life is in His Son”. I wonder what we really know of eternal life.

We would all know that it has been the occasion of crucial conflict, in which God wrought in His grace the victory for Himself and for the truth, when the truth of eternal life was in question. But the truth of eternal life in some sense is very often in question; not so much as to the principles governing it, and what the thing itself really is, but whether we ourselves are in the full experience and enjoyment of it. I suspect that very much more recent conflicts than those of the early 1900’s have as their inward root a loss of appreciation of what eternal life really is, in the experience and blessedness of it. But God has given us witness, to bring us back to this vital thing; if we are not moving; acting, speaking, living in the power of such a life as this, what kind of witness shall be rendered? Witness according to God is in living persons. In what manner of life do they live? The point with God is eternal life—“And this is the witness, that God has given to us eternal life”. Verse 11 points us to Christ as the One in whom that life is. We derive it of necessity from Him; He is the eternal life. That does not mean that the thought is limited to Himself; it means that we come into something which is in Himself, and it is in the Spirit that we do that. But do we, dear brethren, appreciate eternal life? In the very presence of death and the scene on which death is stamped morally, are we in life? Are we drawing upon hidden springs of life according to God, relating us to Christ up there and life in Himself?

But to come back to the earlier verses, “For they that bear witness are three—the Spirit, and the water, and the blood”. Let us refer to those three points again—the Spirit, first, gives us an understanding of the other two, the water, and the blood; the water and the blood flowed, as John himself tells us, from the side of Jesus, dead upon

the cross. These things are to move us, to affect us in our spirits, to affect us in our lives. A total provision has been made for the whole state and condition of man. John gives us this full view of the death of Jesus, a death that was necessary for the clearance of every feature of guilt—that is the blood; a death that was necessary for the putting away of the man that brought in the guilt and death—that is the water. It is witness to the entire necessity for the dying of Jesus, but the necessity alongside of this for the full bearing of His death to be understood and worked out in each one of us; the witness is there, “the Spirit, and the water, and the blood”.

We can always go back to those things, whatever eventuality may arise, however the enemy may seek in his subtlety to get hold of us. Every soul, maybe, knows in secret for himself in what singular ways the enemy seeks to get a hold of him. We use the expression ‘those besetting sins’, and we would all have an understanding with God as to what our besetting sins might be, particular things by which the enemy would seek to entrap us. But we go back to the witness. We can always go back to the witness, and as we do so God delights to bring in a stabilizing touch, because the witness stands whatever else may eventuate—“the Spirit, and the water, and the blood”. I dwell on this point, dear brethren, because of a sense of the need of all of us being stabilised in the understanding of divine things, so that we stand in divine strength in the defence of the truth and in the defence of the rights of Christ. We are to be stabilised in the appreciation of all that He has effected, that He might have His witnesses here, and have them here now.
So it is a question of something “shining forth” against the dark background of Corinthian conditions,

from which, thank God; something was emerging as Paul wrote his second letter. He speaks of this—“Because it is the God who spoke that out of darkness light should shine who has shone, in, our hearts for the shining forth of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ”, a unique verse the very presentation of which may puzzle us; but it conveys what is peculiarly related to what I seek to say, that there is something shining forth from the saints. And what is shining forth is in no sense what may mark them after the flesh; there is no shining forth of that. Nothing will accredit Christ, nothing will accredit the blessed God, if there is something appearing which belongs to our flesh. We are apt to be marked by certain features according to flesh which are in some way characteristic of us— that is not a shining forth; it will tend to diminish and to obstruct the shining forth according to God of what He would bring out in us.

So what is to shine is “the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ”, something neither time nor circumstances here can change. The glory of God has shone. The glory of God shines still. Where does it shine? In the face of Jesus Christ. We can look up into that face, that blessed face, and, save as we are on some very wrong line, we shall be affected by what we see in the face of Jesus Christ, and something will be effected in us of life character. It is a little like what we have at the end of 2 Corinthians 3, where it is a question of change, “transformed according to the same image from glory to glory”. That is, something is set forth in Jesus uniquely; the saints behold it and are affected in like character; and the Spirit is the power and the grace for that effect to appear.
Beloved brethren, to what extent are we affected

as we behold Christ? With the eye of faith we see the glory of the Man in the glory, in the place where God has set Him, the sphere in which He properly belongs—the sphere in which everything is resounding in response to Himself. As we behold Jesus there, is there not some effect in ourselves of the most positive and blessed kind? The face is the part of the organism which conveys peculiar feeling in a sensitive way. We see things in the face of a man which disclose something about that man’s inwards. As you look round on the brethren in the wonderful occasions we have in these closing moments you see something in their faces, and it is positive; it is Christ shining; and that is the divine intent! It might not always be so, mark you. It might be said simply, ‘It is so if it is so’; but the intent of the scripture is that it shall be so.

As we see things brought out in the holy feelings of Jesus, and behold His face, our inwards are to be affected. The Spirit helps us so that our inwards might be affected, and the whole being be affected. This is no time in the testimony for shallowness, as I need scarcely say, and God in His wisdom is allowing much to take place which is searching out shallowness.

The question is arising whether our inwards are reached in their depths, or whether our committals are shallow. I say that as feeling the need of it for myself. The Spirit would reach the depths; He loves to reach the depths. He loves to engage us with Christ, and to go on engaging us with Christ, repeatedly engaging us with Christ, that the depths might be reached and persons thus be secured who are trustworthy and fitting witnesses.

So Paul says here, “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the surpassingness of the power may be of God, and not from us”. How much that scripture, in a very comforting way, encompasses for

us. Why do certain things happen? Why do sorrows arise? Why are there weaknesses, sicknesses, frailties of one kind and another? “We have this treasure in earthen vessels”—it is according to God that it is so. It is glorious that something of Himself be brought out in the sense of witness in such conditions as these, the vital superiority of what God has wrought being brought out—gloriously. He works in the midst of conditions which of themselves involve so much that is hateful to Him; and yet, in the midst of all that, God has something brought out in His own work in those whom He is pleased in His sovereignty to work upon.
The choicest elements related to Christ in glory are brought into expression in the sense of shining here, for the shining is to be in us.

“It is the God who spoke that out of darkness light should shine who has shone in our hearts for the shining forth of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ”. The shining forth is to be noted. It has in mind that (putting it very simply) every one that sees us will see something of the shining forth. The shining forth is appreciated most, I think, in the circle of the saints, the christian circle, where the shining will be assessed at its true value, its true character; the shining forth has in mind that there is something there so distinct, so genuine, so firmly based, that all in some sense can take account of it. We were hearing of a beloved brother in the north who was tested greatly in respect of unions; but eventually he found that the men respected his view; they were prepared to work with him because they recognised that what was in that man was genuine. That is witness, witness to Christ, witness to the truth. There is a shining forth of something in such a case. We may well covet that that may be so with every one of us, that there is a shining forth of something that can fitly take its place as a witness to God, and to Christ.

So in the forty days before the Lord Jesus was taken up the disciples were concerned about things, looking on in their inquiry to the ending up ultimately, of things here. We rightly have that very closely in view; ‘but what shall characterise our pathway in the meantime? It may be an hour, it may be a day, it may be a week, it might be a year; but what shall we do in that time? The Lord turns their minds away from what is just prophetic in character to the great point of the present; and at any moment in the testimony the great point is what is brought forth in the present time. So the Lord says, “It is not yours to know times or seasons, which the Father has placed in his awn authority”; this is a wonderful reference to the Father and His place in supremacy in the economy of love, the Son being in a subject relation to Him.

This is a presentation of the economy to which we belong in the sense of standing related to it, to the Father and to the Son, and to the Spirit; we are attached to it in being of the assembly, the vessel in which the choicest relations of that same economy are brought out.

There are the relations of the Father with His sons, the relations of Christ with His bride, the relations of the Spirit with the bride of Christ and with God’s sons. Do we understand our place in that great economy of love? It would bring in a great range of thought to adorn and strengthen the principle of witness, in which we have part.

So the Lord says, “but ye will receive power”. We come down now to the facts of the immediate situation, which is never out of God’s mind, and how the saints stand in the immediate situation. It is right to be expectant of the Lord’s coming; it is right that we show forth His death until He come; but the Spirit would say, ‘How are you now, in the midst of the present situation on this day?

How do you stand in relation to divine things?’. “But ye will receive power”, the Lord says, “the Holy Spirit having come upon you”. The Lord in His skill and His grace diverts a certain line of thought among the disciples to the prime point of the moment, which is the Holy Spirit. We have had much ministry about the Spirit. We have had many an injunction to give the Spirit greater place, and to seek Him personally in a more distinct and definite way. I would only seek in a word like this to add to those injunctions, that we may heed the glorious fact of the Spirit being here in the assembly, and immediately available to sustain, strengthen and maintain what is according to God. No witness will be true witness that does not know the Spirit as the power for it.

Then He says, “and ye shall be my witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. And having said these things he was taken up”, as if He had just given them exactly the present position. Then He goes up, and leaves them in the hand of the Spirit. The proposition He makes is that they should be His witnesses. Think of what these men had seen in Jesus, what they had experienced in their times with Jesus. Let us remind ourselves that when the number of the apostles was made up to twelve, a little later than this, the necessary basis of anyone to be thus appointed was that he had been with them as Jesus went in and out amongst them, all the time from John’s baptism to His being taken up. There was to be a basis for witness in a personal, deep appreciation of Christ. The whole of what came out in that glorious Man was really essential to the witness of the twelve, and whilst we are not of the twelve we come in on the line of the testimony which the twelve set on, under the hand of God, and which the Spirit has sustained. The principle of witness remains still and we are to be His witnesses. The Lord does not expand what that will mean in detail; He does not tell them where to go; He shows that the field of the testimony is a very wide one, and He proceeds in the Acts to send out His beloved ones into it. He is not telling them here exactly what it would be, but that they were to be His witnesses.

I would like to leave that impression with us, that the point is to be His witnesses. There may be many varieties of circumstance in which we are placed in which it is to appear—but the point is we are witnesses to Christ. We are witnesses to that glorious Man up there. We are not witnesses to anything less than what God has established in the Person of Christ, as He is and where He is. So may our witness be distinct, beloved brethren, beginning as we take account of the witness that God has given us, the understanding of “the Spirit, and the water, and the blood”, and the witness to eternal life; for that life must be surging in us if the witness is to gain in power. May God help us in these things, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: HOW WE HAVE ACCESS TO THE FATHER
articles.author: E. M. Walkinshaw

paragraphs.text: I was thinking, dear brethren, of the wonderful fact of our having been made nigh and having access through Christ by one Spirit to the Father. The privilege is very great and it belongs to all believers. I think the Lord would encourage us to take it up. Paul speaks here to these Ephesians who had been aliens from the commonwealth of Israel. They were not to forget what they once were in the flesh, that they were alienated from everything that was precious—very much like the younger son who had gone into the far country—gone away from God, abandoned Him, and found themselves in idolatry and distance. God comes in in His wonderful grace, and His disposition is towards all men, not just towards the Jew. Christ Jesus is the Mediator of God and men (1 Timothy 2: 5), not of God and the Jews. It is not a function just toward Jew or gentile; what is before God is men.

So here Paul exhorts them to remember what they had been, complete strangers to everything that was precious to God, and, in fact, at that time, precious to the Jew. Then Paul says, “But now in Christ Jesus ye who once were afar off are become nigh by the blood of the Christ”. I think that is a very touching statement. It refers really to the giving up of the life of Him who is the Head of the anointed system, and in the giving up of His life He has removed for ever the order of man which was displeasing to God. So we have a reference to His blood, and to being made nigh. I think that is moral. It is how we are to understand it, dear brethren, that it cost Jesus His precious life.

He had to give up His life, and His blood be shed, in order that we who were afar off might become nigh, and we are become nigh in Christ Jesus. It is not that the flesh is made nigh, or the gentile made nigh, but “now in Christ Jesus ye … are become nigh”. It is in Christ Jesus, that is, another Man. I believe God would help us to lay hold of this so that we might be strengthened in what He has done, that in the blood of Christ every moral issue has been met and the man who was so displeasing to God removed, and we, although gentiles, have, as persons, been brought into nearness to, and favour with, God. How wonderful it is! There was a time when we were without Christ, having no hope, and without God in the world; now we are not thus in the world. I think God would have us to appreciate that, and to appreciate what it cost that we might become nigh.

I think of the father’s affections for that son who went into the far country; his affections were very real, and never changed. The prodigal was ever his son, although distant from him, but in coming back on the wonderful ground of repentance he came into the favour that was his. I think the spirit of repentance is to mark us all the time—a change of mind. It is not just a question of something that happened twenty, thirty, or forty years ago, although, of course, that was very real and necessary—“repentance towards God, and faith towards our Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 20: 21)—but I think it is a question all the time. A constant change of mind brings us into a deeper appreciation of the Person and the work of Christ, and consequently into the enjoyment of our nearness to God. As I

said, I think that is moral, but access by one Spirit is spiritual. I put the two together so that we might see something of the difference, but the moral foundation in the blood of Christ lays the basis for what is spiritual, and, as we all know in our exercises, what is moral must necessarily precede what is spiritual.

Then Paul goes on to say, “For he is our peace”. He is dealing, of course, with the distance and enmity which existed between the Jew and the gentile. There might be enmity existing between rich and poor, or between different social classes, between brother and brother, or sister and sister, but the fact is that that kind of man has been completely removed. So Paul says, “He is our peace”. It is not God’s peace here, it is our peace. Paul says in another passage, “having made peace by the blood of his cross” (Colossians 1: 20); I think that refers to peace for the Godhead. But here he says He, that is Christ, is our peace. Think of the middle wall of enclosure being broken down; the distance that existed, the enmity, the hatred between Jew and gentile, completely broken down. It is not, as another has said, that the Jew is brought down to the level of the gentile, or that the gentile is brought up to the level of the Jew—morally both are removed. So whatever alienation existed, or may exist even today, is not settled by the one being brought down to the level of the other, or the other being brought up to the level of the one, but by both morally being removed. Both Jew and gentile have been removed morally from under the eye of God, and Christ has formed the two in Himself into one new man.
Now, dear brethren, that one new man is Christ in character in the saints, and He has reconciled both Jew and gentile in one body to God. So we can

see how in the precious work of Christ, His blood, His flesh, the cross, everything that stood in the way has been completely removed; not only that which stood in the way between us and God, but anything that might stand in the way between brother and brother and sister and sister, so that the enmity has gone. It speaks here of His blood, as I have said, and it speaks also of His flesh. You will notice what is said, He has “broken down the middle wall of enclosure, having annulled the enmity in his flesh, the law of commandments in ordinances, that he might form the two in himself into one new man, making peace”. So that what is in mind through the work of Christ, and the Person of Christ, is that both should in perfect harmony and in perfect peace have access to the Father. I think it is very touching, dear brethren, and it should affect our hearts and help us to judge ourselves in the light of the precious death of Jesus, so that as we judge ourselves we are able together, as one, to enter into the presence of the Father. One has always been touched in reading this passage by the reference to His blood, and to His flesh, and to the cross—what it cost the Lord Jesus so that the middle wall of enclosure might be broken down, and that applies morally wherever it may apply.

Today it hardly applies to Jew and gentile because mainly in the assembly we have nations, or gentiles, but it does, of course, apply socially very often. At one time the rich sat in one place in the meeting and the poor in another. We might be horrified at that and hardly believe that it was the case, but it was. But the Lord in His gracious operations has, I believe, gradually brought the brethren into correspondence with the truth so that they appreciate that in His death both the poor and the rich were morally extinguished. The poor are not made rich, nor are the rich made poor. If in

God’s ways I am poor, I remain poor. If another brother is rich, he remains rich. But morally there is no difference. In the assembly in Christ Jesus we are all one, and I think the Spirit of God would help us to reach that.

So as I have said, as we get a touch as to the blood of Christ, the flesh of Christ, and the cross of Christ, it becomes a lever in our souls to judge ourselves so that we might not only be reconciled to God, but reconciled to one another, and thus experience access through Christ by one Spirit to the Father. So that first of all there is His blood, then His flesh, then the cross, and then Himself. So the work is there—He has done everything that was necessary; He has made the way morally; but we have not only what is moral dealt with, we also have the Spirit.

We have Christ’s work, and His Person, and through Him, in that permanent, glorious, mediatorial position, we have access in the power of one Spirit to the Father. So, dear brethren, we both go in—that is the idea. Jew and gentile both go in. You may say, ‘How can it be?’. It can only be because God has so wrought to bring persons into the gain of the death of Jesus that together they can both go in in one new man, that is Christ in character under the eye of God. So we should take up this privilege. As I have already said, it belongs to every believer. No matter where he is, how distant he may be, it is his property. Now the point is, Can I take it up? Can I take up the access that Christ has won for me? Can I appreciate the moral side, that is, His blood, His flesh, the cross? Then can I appreciate Himself, and the presence of the Spirit, so that you and I, and the brethren, can together take up the greatest privilege that you could possibly imagine for men and women here? I would agree that it is not as men and women spiritually, but men and women here are able to take up
the greatest possible privilege—access to the Father.

I think the opening up of that, and the Father’s realm, is in chapter three, the Father supreme in a world of bliss that has breadth, and length, and depth, and height; but if we are to enjoy it, dear brethren, we must face with God the moral side, judging ourselves, so that we are in correspondence with the death of Jesus and able to take up the privileges that belong to us.
May we be encouraged to do it, for His name’s sake.
I seek the help of the Spirit, dear brethren, to pass on a simple impression as to these scriptures which refer to the idea of the full result that God is going to secure, as we sang in our hymn—
‘The harvest’s full increase
Be God’s for evermore’.

We are accustomed in our day to the narrowing down of things as they appear to us outwardly but I believe the Spirit would help us to have our eyes opened to see the great and glorious fulness of God’s thoughts. These scriptures refer to the many brethren, to the many sons, and to going up to the house of God amid the throng, and I believe it would encourage our hearts to take account of what it is God’s purpose to secure. If God purposes that there should be many

brethren, of whom Christ shall be the Firstborn, and if He purposes that there shall be many sons brought to glory, we can be assured that there will indeed be a full result for His own glory eternally.
We generally think of the idea of going with the crowd as being something that is not good.
To be carried along with the stream of the influences that are abroad in the world would certainly carry us in the wrong direction, but there is a stream of which the psalmist speaks—
“There is a river the streams whereof make glad the city of God”, Psalm 46: 4. There is that which is gathering in fulness, which has all been secured through the precious work of Christ.
It has all been gathered up and all will be made to yield for God’s glory.

What a favour, beloved brethren, to be found amongst the many brethren. What the apostle speaks of in Romans 8 is almost beyond our apprehension; we have been predestinated to be conformed to the image of God’s Son. Mr. Darby in his hymn wondered at such purposes of God in blessing—
‘And is it so? I shall be like Thy Son!
Is this the grace which He for me has won?
Father of glory! Thought beyond all thought;
In glory to His own blest likeness brought’.

Wonderful as is our portion—and it would do us good, I think, to ponder worshipfully, as Mr. Darby did, upon the blessedness of divine grace that would give us such a portion—the point and purpose of the verse seems to be that there should be many brethren among whom He should be the Firstborn. How right it is that He should thus stand out. In the midst of a vast company His position is rightly to be seen. “As the apple-tree among the trees of the wood.

So is my beloved among the sons”, Song of Solomon 2: 3. How our hearts rejoice, beloved brethren, at the full result that is assured, that is for the bringing into pre-eminence of the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.

The verse in Hebrews 2 is on the same line, again presenting what to our human minds are the imponderable workings of God. It says, “For it became him … in bringing many sons to glory …”. It has been God’s pleasure to operate in this way. “It became him”; such is God’s nature, such is He, that it is suitable that He should operate in this way in His delight, to have men before Him in acceptability, in joy and suitability, and in all the dignity of sonship. But it is many sons. God’s delight is to have His house full, and we are given a part amongst the many sons brought to glory. Again what is stressed is the pre-eminence of Christ, the One who is the Leader of our salvation. This expression as to His being made perfect calls attention to the wonderful ability He has—one hesitates to use such language—and how absolutely qualified He is to present everything to the Father. How He delights to take up what is spoken of in the later verses, this wonderful position of singing God’s praises in the midst of the assembly. How pre-eminent He is; everything depends upon Him, everything is assured as depending upon the One who has made this wonderful salvation possible, the One who is carrying through now what will yield a full result for God’s eternal pleasure. How delightful these expressions are as to singing God’s praises in the midst of the assembly. The assembly itself, I suppose, conveys to our minds the fulness of what God has secured. We are reminded in Ephesians 1: 23 that it is “the fulness of him who fills all in all”. We had a thought as to that on Lord’s day as to what is conveyed in the assembly, the vessel which is to be filled with God’s praise.
The verse in Psalm 55 has always had an appeal

to me, although it is in a negative and very solemn setting. But there is something very positive in the thought of walking to the house of God amid the throng. As our brother has said, what greater privilege could there be for man to enter into than to have access through Christ by one Spirit to the Father? and as we have been reminded it is in mind that we should enter together into this wonderful privilege. As rightly understood, what a joy it is to move together amid the throng! We understand that there are holy myriads secured for God’s pleasure and that this portion is open to us to walk amid the throng. It suggests an ease in our hearts and minds, understanding that it is the pleasure of God that we all should go up in this worshipful way. I suppose it refers to the times when the children of Israel went up year by year to Jerusalem. What a period of joy it was, and under normal conditions everything would be right.

I believe there is an appeal to us in this verse, yet a solemn warning. As we take up this privilege, as moving together to the house of God, the question is raised with us as to whether there is anything that partakes of the character that was found in the betrayer, of whom this passage speaks, whether things are right with us as we go up. It is a terrible thing to be carried along in an unreal way but, beloved brethren, what a joy it is to take account of what is normal, the way God would have us to be happy in our souls as we merge together amid the throng. We would not be unduly occupied with the smallness of things that may press upon us outwardly, but would have large impressions of all that God has secured in which He is to be glorified eternally. May the Lord enlarge our apprehension of these things, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: “THE TEACHER IS COME AND CALLS THEE”
articles.author: C. R. Byng
articles.meeting: Word at the burial of our sister Mrs, A. Strugnell

paragraphs.text: This was a very precious message that was entrusted to Martha, and a very precious message to be received by Mary—“The teacher is come and calls thee”. Our beloved sister had an even greater privilege—the Teacher Himself came and called her. His eye and touch have been over our beloved sister through a long life; especially during the days of all the weeks of her limitation and bodily frailty His eye had been upon her and He valued her patience, grace, and perseverance, her love for her husband, for the saints, for the testimony. He had taken account of all that and the moment came in the perfection of divine timing when the Teacher Himself came and called her. Whilst, as we have said, as regards things in this life, she fell asleep in Jesus, we can also be assured that in her spirit she was immediately responsive to His call. So it says that Mary “when she heard that, rises up quickly and comes to him”. What a moment for our beloved sister, to be with Christ, the One that she loved and had known; she heard the voice of Jesus as He came for her and she went to Him.

But the same Teacher, beloved brethren, would speak to us today. The Spirit as being with us would give us the assurance that He would say to each of us that He is calling us. The message came “secretly”. That is not, of course, any lack of transparency, the Lord Jesus never does anything like that; this was an intensely personal matter which was not known even by those around.

The Spirit would bring this voice to each of us, privately and personally, at this time of sorrow, that the Teacher is calling; He “is come and calls thee”. What a Teacher He is! It is one of the great and glorious titles of the Word. He is in Himself the full expression of every thought of the mind and heart of God, and yet as the Teacher how close He comes to bring us into the gain of all the purposes of God.

He is the Shepherd and the Teacher. Every disciple comes under His personal touch. “It is sufficient”, the Lord said, “for the disciple that he should become as his teacher”, Matthew 10: 25. What a privilege we have, each of us, as disciples to have to do with Him personally, the One who is bringing us moment by moment more into the glorious experience of what is beyond death. How graciously, how clearly, how powerfully, He teaches, and His teaching is so powerful because He expresses everything in Himself. If He teaches us the truth about resurrection, He says “I am the resurrection” (John 11: 25). So if Abraham was assured, we can be assured. We can be assured when we think of the reality of burial that for our beloved sister it is only a very temporary matter, just for a moment it may be, until the Lord with an assembling shout will call all the dead in Christ. They will all arise for they will all hear the assembling shout. His voice will be heard and we shall all go up together, maybe even this day. Let us be alert; the Teacher’s voice is penetrating through; let us be waiting for it.
In the meantime, if He does leave us here, He would call us into greater communion with Himself. Mary went to be with Him where He was. He would

call each of us today to be with Him in an increased appreciation of Himself and an increased enjoyment of His love; to be with Him where He is beyond the reach of death and sorrows, in a scene where there is no more sea and no more tears. In this period of sorrow He teaches us so that we may not be attached to this scene, but be attached to Him in a scene of glory where He is going to be eternally. We can surely say, ‘Hallelujah”. We are going to be with Him for ever!

The Spirit would bring the power and attraction of the gracious love of Jesus to each one of us at this time to draw us closer to Himself. It was the Mary who went out to Jesus where He was who had the grace to anoint Jesus so that the odour of the ointment filled the house. May our experience with Jesus increasingly help us to give Him just the touch He needs in this waiting time. He waited for our sister, and then He called her. He is waiting for us and He is going to call us very soon. In the meantime may we be nearer to Him, to prove His love, and to yield to Him for His own pleasure, for His name’s sake.

“LET HIM SELL HIS GARMENT AND BUY A SWORD” These words of the Lord in Luke 22: 36 are striking, pointing to the need to dispose of certain things if the Holy Spirit’s power is to be experienced. An older man might feel that he has a certain experience and status and just rely on that. If he does, he will lack

power and effectiveness. Far better to sell his garment and buy a sword. Then, as he is in faith and dependence, the unmistakable power of the Spirit will be manifest. A young man may have a clear mind and good powers of expression, and rely on that. Better to sell that garment and buy a sword. Then, as Paul, says, it will be “not the word ... but the power”, 1

Corinthians 4: 19. Paul had thoroughly worked out this matter. He says that his word and his preaching were “not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power”, 1 Corinthians 2: 4. He had sold his garment and bought a sword.

I would say to young christians, Mention His name; it does not matter how you say it. Do not say, ‘I am not interested’, when asked to read a novel, or to go to the pictures; do not get out of it by a backdoor way; it is missing a privilege. Mention His name and never mind how stumblingly and weakly you do it; you may shake like an aspen leaf but get His name out.
Say why you do not go to the pictures. Mention His name; you hoist the flag of the kingdom then, and all the power of the kingdom will support you.
